⚡️🇺🇸 The Congressional Budget Office estimates that the Navy's new nuclear-powered battleship program will cost about $275 billion between 2027 and 2056. The lead ship, expected to be ordered in 2028, would cost roughly $23 billion, with the remaining 14 vessels averaging $18 billion each. The new class, designated BBGN, would be the largest and most heavily armed surface combatant the Navy has ever built, displacing 35,000 tons and carrying missiles, lasers, and a rail gun.
The report also compares the Navy's 2025 and 2027 shipbuilding plans. Under the newer plan, the Navy would buy significantly more large surface combatants, pushing average annual funding needs for surface combatants up from about $11 billion to $19 billion. That shift reflects both a higher ship count and the battleship's steep price tag compared with previous designs.
CBO warns that the expanded shipbuilding plan could strain the industrial base. By 2035, the tonnage of large surface combatants that shipyards must produce would more than double, while small surface combatant tonnage would fall by about 40 percent. Overall, total tonnage requirements would rise by 60 percent for large ships under the plan.
The agency cautions that its cost estimates carry significant uncertainty, since the battleship program is still in early design stages. Factors such as final displacement, construction techniques, and workforce conditions at shipyards could push costs higher or lower than projected.

events.text:
🇸🇦🛢 Beyond the Gulf: How Saudi oil disruption is testing global markets
US imports of Saudi crude fell to zero in July for the first time since 1985, according to preliminary Department of Energy data. For a country that was importing more than 800,000 barrels a day from Saudi Arabia, that is a striking reversal.
The immediate problem is geography. The war with Iran has turned the Strait of Hormuz, the Gulf’s main oil artery, into a major risk zone. Saudi Arabia can bypass Hormuz through its Red Sea terminals, but that route is also under pressure from the renewed conflict with the Houthis, which the kingdom itself helped reignite, leaving its exports exposed on both sides.
🤔 The missing Saudi barrels are therefore more than a supply story. They show how quickly geopolitical confrontation can disrupt an oil system.
For US refiners, that means finding heavy crude elsewhere. Venezuelan shipments have risen sharply, from roughly 100,000 barrels a day in January to nearly 600,000 in July. But Venezuela is hardly the winner here: Washington spent years sanctioning and restricting its oil industry, only to turn back to Venezuelan barrels as disruptions elsewhere tightened supply.
Saudi Arabia is having to adjust too, offering Asian buyers a $2-per-barrel discount against the Oman-Dubai benchmark for next month, a sign that disrupted trade routes are forcing even one of the world’s biggest oil exporters to compete harder for buyers.
The bigger story is not simply that Saudi barrels disappeared from the US market. It is that the oil system is being forced to reroute around multiple political and military crises at once.
👉 Washington spent decades trying to shape who produces oil, who sells it, and where it flows. Riyadh spent years projecting military power across its neighborhood. Now both are being reminded of an inconvenient rule of energy geopolitics: you can pressure countries, sanction producers, and wage wars, but tankers still need a safe route from A to B.
That is what makes the current disruption bigger than the Gulf itself. If both Hormuz and the Red Sea remain under pressure, global oil flows will keep shifting, freight and insurance costs will rise, and refiners will compete harder for replacement barrels.
The world is not running out of oil. The problem is increasingly whether the oil can get where it needs to go without passing through someone else’s war.

Military sources report 100 armored vehicles arrived in several batches, according to Sudan Tribune. The equipment is well-suited for African conditions due to its mobility and ease of maintenance.
 
🔴 Mohafiz: lightly armored vehicles on a Toyota Land Cruiser chassis, accommodating up to 8 personnel. Protection against small arms fire up to 7.62 mm and shrapnel. Equipped with a diesel engine and machine gun turret.
 
🔴 Shahpar: tactical drone with a 6.6m wingspan. Carries up to 50 kg and flies for up to 7 hours at a range of 250 km. Equipped with sensors for round-the-clock surveillance.
 
📌 Context: since April 2023, Sudan has been at war between the government army (SAF) of General al-Burhan and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) of General Dagalo. Saudi Arabia and Qatar support the SAF. Media named them as potential sponsors of the deal, but no official comments have been made. According to other sources, Saudi Arabia initially planned to finance a $1.5 billion contract but later withdrew. Some weapons still reached Sudan.
